name: Graphene
summary: The oldest Python GraphQL library: code first, with its own field classes such as `graphene.String` and a `resolve_` method per field.
intro: Graphene is code first, but not built on type hints. You subclass `graphene.ObjectType` and declare each field as a class attribute holding a Graphene type: `title = graphene.String(required=True)` becomes `title: String!`, and `book = graphene.Field(Book)` points at another type. Arguments are declared the same way, and their snake_case names become camelCase in the schema, so `first_name` turns into `firstName`. Each field can have a resolver method named `resolve_<field>`, which gets the parent value, an `info` object and the arguments. `graphene.Schema(query=Query)` builds a GraphQL-core schema, and `schema.execute()` runs a query against it. Relay support (nodes, connections and mutations) is built in, and separate packages connect it to Django, SQLAlchemy and MongoDB models and to Apollo Federation.

Graphene 3 (November 2021) moved onto GraphQL-core 3, added subscriptions and dropped Python 2. Since then development has slowed: the latest release is 3.4.3 from November 2024, also the latest commit, and its README asks for contributors. It requires `graphql-core` older than 3.3, so it stays on the 3.2 line that follows GraphQL.js 16. Graphene itself has no web server. Starlette once shipped a `GraphQLApp` for it but deprecated it, and the FastAPI docs point to the third-party `starlette-graphene3` package, whose repository was last updated in September 2023, while recommending Strawberry for new projects.
strengths: Mature, with a large ecosystem: graphene-django, graphene-sqlalchemy, graphene-mongo and graphene-federation build types from existing models
Built-in Relay support: nodes with global IDs, cursor connections and Relay-style mutations
Code first: no SDL file to keep in sync, and snake_case Python maps to camelCase GraphQL automatically
Spec-compliant schemas that work with any GraphQL client, such as Relay, Apollo and gql
limits: Little recent development: no release or commit since November 2024
Pinned to `graphql-core` below 3.3, so it can’t use GraphQL.js 17 features such as `@defer` and `@stream`
Field types are Graphene objects, not Python type hints, so the schema and your type annotations are written separately
No ASGI server of its own: FastAPI and Starlette need the third-party `starlette-graphene3`, itself untouched since 2023

story: Facebook published the GraphQL spec in July 2015. In October 2015 Syrus Akbary released Graphene, together with `graphql-core`, Akbary’s Python port of GraphQL.js. By December 2015 it had Django support, and SQLAlchemy followed in January 2016. For about three years it was Python’s only real GraphQL library. Graphene 1.0 (September 2016) was announced as production ready, and Graphene 2.0 (October 2017) simplified how types are implemented.

Akbary later handed maintenance to members of the GraphQL-Python community. Graphene 3.0, in November 2021, rebuilt it on GraphQL-core 3, the modern port of GraphQL.js, added subscriptions and better enums, and dropped Python 2. By then Strawberry and Ariadne had arrived, and FastAPI’s docs now recommend Strawberry. Releases continued until 3.4.3 in November 2024.

choices.choice: Code first, with its own type classes
choices.why: Instead of writing SDL, you describe the schema in Python. In 2015 type hints had only just arrived (Python 3.5) and `dataclasses` only arrived later, in Python 3.7, so fields are Graphene objects that carry their GraphQL type, arguments and options.

Relay, Facebook’s GraphQL client, has its own specifications for global object identification and cursor connections. Graphene provides nodes, connections and mutations that follow them, so a Python API works with Relay directly.

choices.choice: Data agnostic, with integrations as add-ons
choices.why: Graphene works with any data source, from Django and SQLAlchemy models to plain Python objects. Model integrations live in separate packages, such as graphene-django and graphene-sqlalchemy.

timeline.text: First release by Syrus Akbary in October
SQLAlchemy support in January; 1.0 in September
